## HW 2 Summary

- There were lots of choices:
  - To impute parental education or not
  - To log transform earnings or not

## To Impute or Not to Impute....

- Depends on why variables are missing
  - Missing Completely At Random- dropping is ok
  - Some characteristic is different about missing- imputation might be needed
  - Missingness related to value of variable (hard)

## 'log' transform earnings?

- Most said yes
  - Generally wise choice
  - Otherwise need weighted least squares
  - It _is_ interpretable!


## Earnings = 0?

- Biggest Challenge of 'log' transform
  - Option 1: Drop the 0 values
  - Option 2: Add nominal value to earnings

## Drop the 0 Values?

- Censored/truncated outcome bias
- Must interpret model differently
- Major problem in social sciences data

## Add a constant?

- Adding a constant will add a "point mass" in left tail
- Biases your parameter estimates

![https://aosmith.rbind.io/2018/09/19/the-log-0-problem/](log0.png)


## Add a constant?

- Adding a constant will add a "point mass" in left tail
- Biases your parameter estimates

![https://aosmith.rbind.io/2018/09/19/the-log-0-problem/](logtable.png)


## Gold Standard

- Given covariates $\mathbf{x}$, model two things: 
  - $p(y=0|\mathbf{x}$, i.e. probability of 0 
  - $p(y|\mathbf{x},\, y>0)$, i.e. combine with the drop model


## Two Stage Model
  - logistic regression for $y=0$: 
$$
p(y=0|\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(\sum_{j=0}^p \beta_j x_j)}
$$
  - log-linear regression for $y>0$
$$
p(\log(y)|\mathbf{x},y>0) \sim \mathrm{normal}\left(\sum_{j=0}^p w_jx_j,\sigma^2\right)
$$


## What if the zeros are caused by an important unobserved variable

- eg a health condition that effects low wage workers more than high wage workers
- 2000 Nobel Prize in Econ for Heckman Correction
- Very generic and powerful technique, applies more broadly


## Forward/Backward Selection?

- Can get stuck in a local minimum
- Best: Use expert knowledge a design few models
- Never use it for inference


![](var_selection.png)





## Types of errors

- Credit dataset:
    - Defaults rare, Bayes decision rule predicts no defaults!
    - False Negative: predicted no default, default happened
    - False Positive: predicted default, no default happened

## Decision Thresholds

- Consequences of mistakes can vary:
  - Predict rain wrong you accidentally carried umbrella
  - Predict sun wrong, you arrived to work soaked

::: {style="border: 2px solid black; padding: 20px; border-radius: 5px;"}
__Solution:__ Bias your prediction away from the mistake that has worse consequences
:::


## ROC Curve

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width=50%}
```{python}



default = islp.load_data('Default')
train_set, test_set = train_test_split(default, test_size=0.2, random_state=123155,stratify=default["default"])



train_set_target = train_set["default"].copy()
test_set_target = test_set["default"].copy()

le = LabelEncoder()
y_train = le.fit_transform(train_set_target)
y_test = le.transform(test_set_target)

train_set_drop = train_set.copy().drop(["default"],axis=1)
test_set_drop = test_set.copy().drop(["default"],axis=1)

numerical_features = ["balance","income"]

categorical_features = ["student"]

preprocessor = ColumnTransformer([
    ('num', StandardScaler(), numerical_features),
    ('cat', OneHotEncoder(drop='first', handle_unknown='ignore', sparse_output=False), categorical_features)
])  

pipe_lr = Pipeline([
    ('prep', preprocessor),
    ('model', LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
])

pipe_lr.fit(train_set_drop,y_train)

model_lr_f = pipe_lr.named_steps['model']

def logistic_features(pipe):
    
    model = pipe.named_steps['model']
    preprocessor = pipe.named_steps['prep']
    
    feature_names = preprocessor.get_feature_names_out()

    coef_df = pd.DataFrame({
        'feature': list(feature_names),
        'coefficient': list(model.coef_[0])
    })

    coef_df['odds_ratio'] = np.exp(coef_df['coefficient'])
    coef_df['abs_coefficient'] = coef_df['coefficient'].abs()
    coef_df = coef_df.sort_values('abs_coefficient', ascending=False)
    return coef_df



y_prob = pipe_lr.predict_proba(test_set_drop)[:, 1]

fig, ax = subplots(figsize=(8, 6))

RocCurveDisplay.from_predictions(y_test, y_prob, ax=ax);
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], linestyle="--", color="gray")
ax.set_title("ROC Curve", fontsize=20)
ax.set_xlabel("False Positive Rate", fontsize=16)
ax.set_ylabel("True Positive Rate", fontsize=16);

plt.tight_layout();
plt.show();
```

## Confusion Matrix

- Tabular counterpart to ROC curve
- Displays amount of different types of errors and successes

```{python}


threshold = 0.5
y_pred = (y_prob >= threshold).astype(int)

print("Bayes Decision Rule\n")
print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred, target_names=["No Default", "Default"]))

```


## Confusion Matrix

- Precision: If model said it, was it really true? 

$$
p(y=1|g(\mathbf{x})=1)
$$

- Recall: If it was true, did the model say it? (TPR)
  - _Power_, _Sensitivity_, _Detection Probability_
$$
p(g(\mathbf{x})=1|y=1)
$$

## Confusion Matrix

## Generative versus Discriminative Models

- Discriminative Model: Tell me $\mathbf{x}$, and I will tell you $p(y|\mathbf{x})$
  - Logistic Regression
- Generative Model: I want the joint probability $p(\mathbf{x},y)$
  - Data Generating Process


## Generative versus Discriminative

- Classify coints at vending machine
- Discriminative model learns decision boundary with $p(y|\mathbf{x})$

![](coin_discriminative.png)


## Generative versus Discriminative

- Classify coints at vending machine
- Generative starts with distribution of each class $p(\mathbf{x}|y)$

![](coin_generative.png)

## Generative versus Discriminative

- Classify coints at vending machine
- Generative also considers abundance of classes $p(y)$

![](coin_prior.png)


## Bayes Theorem 

- Chain rule of probability:
$$
p(\mathbf{x},y) = p(\mathbf{x}|y)p(y) = p(y|\mathbf{x})p(\mathbf{x})
$$
- Leads to Bayes Theorem
$$
p(y|\mathbf{x}) = \frac{p(\mathbf{x}|y)p(y)}{p(\mathbf{x})}
$$


## Classification with Generative Model

- We don't need to know $p(\mathbf{x})$ to determine best class
$$
g(\mathbf{x}) = \mathrm{argmax}_y p(\mathbf{x}|y)p(y)
$$

- Or whatever threshold you would like to use for the classes


## Examples of Generative Models

- Linear and Quadratic Discriminant Analysis
- Naive Bayes
- Many types of neural network models:
  - GANs, VAEs, LLMs, Diffusion Models
- Many other powerful ML models, Kernel Density Estimation, LDA, some GPs, etc


## Advantages of Generative Models

- They work better with lower data 

![Ng and Jordan 2002](nb_lr.png)



## Advantages of Generative Models

- Interpretability: You have a model of each class
- Can generate new examples- it is the main application of LLMs

![](chatgpt.png)

- Can incorporate prior knowledge

## Advantages of Generative Models

- More naturally handle missing data through marginalization
- If $x_1$ is missing during prediction, just integrate it out:
$$
p(x_2,x_3,\cdots,x_p|y) = \int dx_1 p(x_1,x_2,\cdots,x_p|y)
$$
- Or if discrete:
$$
p(x_2,x_3,\cdots,x_p|y) = \sum_{x_1\in\mathcal{X}} p(x_1,x_2,\cdots,x_p|y)
$$
- How easy this is depends on your model


## Disadvantages

- Learning $p(\mathbf{x}|y)$ is hard
- Usually need simplifying assumptions, can go wrong



## Disadvantages

- Asymptotically, discriminative classifiers often win:

![Ng and Jordan 2022](nb_lr.png)



## Naive Bayes

- Stupid looking but very successful method
- Features are conditionally independent give the class:

![wikipedia](naivebayes.png)


## Naive Bayes

- Stupid looking but very successful method
- Features are conditionally independent give the class:
$$
p(\mathbf{x}|y) = p(x_1|y)p(x_2|y)\cdots p(x_p|y) 
$$
- prior $p(y)$ comes from observed classes or could be chosen by you
$$
p(y) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n I(y=y_i) 
$$


## Conditional Independence

- $x_1$ and $x_2$ are _conditionally independent_ given $y$ if:
$$
p(x_1|x_2,y) = p(x_1|y)
$$


## Conditional Independence

- Consider _rain_,_thunder_, and _lightning_
- _rain_ and _thunder_ are not independent
$$
p(R|T) \neq P(R)
$$


## Conditional Independence

::: {style="border: 2px solid black; padding: 20px; border-radius: 5px;"}
If I see lighting, then hearing thunder doesn't give me additional information about rain
:::

$$
P(R|T,L) = P(R|L)
$$

- Rain is conditionally independent of thunder given lighting


## Power of Conditional Independence

- Suppose $y$ and all the $x_i$ have two classes each
- Let there be $100$ features
- Need a parameter for each combination of the 100 fetures!
- $2(2^p-1) = 10^{30}$ parameters
- Number of water molecules in one million water bottles


## Power of Conditional Independence

- Suppose $y$ and all the $x_i$ have two classes each
- Let there be $100$ features
- Naive Bayes: 2 parameters per feature
- 200 total!


## Features and Distributions

- $x_i$ is discrete:
  - Each class has a probability
- $x_i$ is continuous:
  - Need to pick a family of distributions!
  - Gaussian Naive Bayes: $ x_i \sim \mathrm{normal}\left(\mu_i,\sigma_i\right)$
  - You may choose other distributions


## Training

- Because of conditional independence, each distribution is fit independently
- Usually with maximum likelihood
- Training observations of class $y$: $\mathcal{D}_y = \{j : y_j = y\}$ 
- $n_y = |\mathcal{D}_y|$ number of data for that class

**Binary Features:**
$$
\hat{p}(x_i = 1 \mid y) = \frac{1}{n_y}\sum_{j \in \mathcal{D}_y} \mathbf{1}(x_{ji} = 1)
$$


## Training

- Because of conditional independence, each distribution is fit independently
- Usually with maximum likelihood
- Training observations of class $y$: $\mathcal{D}_y = \{j : y_j = y\}$ 
- $n_y = |\mathcal{D}_y|$ number of data for that class

**Gaussian likelihood (continuous features):**
$$
\hat{\mu}_{iy} = \frac{1}{n_y}\sum_{j \in \mathcal{D}_y} x_{ji}
\qquad
\hat{\sigma}^2_{iy} = \frac{1}{n_y - 1}\sum_{j \in \mathcal{D}_y} (x_{ji} - \hat{\mu}_{iy})^2
$$


## Laplace Smoothing

- If there are no examples of a potential value of a feature vector corresponding to a class, the predicted probability will be zero
- Laplace smoothing: Add a dummy observation of each value for each class
- 'sklearn' does this by default


## Advantages

- Very fast to train (can constantly update model)
- Can handle huge numbers of features
- Low variance (though high bias)
- Direct interpretability
- Low data requirements

## Disadvantages

- Conditional Independence never true
- Bad calibration
- More complex models outperform it when data is rich


## Misconception

::: {style="border: 2px solid black; padding: 20px; border-radius: 5px;"}
__There is nothing Bayesian about Naive Bayes!__
:::

- Bayesian methods are all about using probabilities to express uncertainty about model parameters
- Naive Bayes just picks them

## Applications

- Spam Filtering!
- Common in medical diagnostics
- Common in insurance/credit due to interpretability
- Bioinformatics (very high dimensional feature space)
- Recommender Systems when time is critical (can handle missing features, train and predict quickly)

## Interpretation

- In binary features case, compute odds ratios
$$
\underbrace{\frac{p(x=1|y=1)}{p(x=1|y=0)}}_{\text{lr for x=1}} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{p(x=0|y=0)}{p(x=0|y=1)}}_{\text{lr for x=0}}
$$


## Interpretation

- In continuous case, depends on distributions and your choices
- For each feature get a Gaussian for each class
![mlstory.org](haystack.png)


## Signal to Noise Ratio

- For two Gaussians, Signal to Noise Ratio is:
$$
SNR = \frac{|\mu_0-\mu_1|}{\sqrt{\sigma_1^0+\sigma_1^2}}
$$



## SNR and Performance

- SNR Determines Shape of ROC Curve

![mlstory.org](snr.png)




## Signal To Noise Ratio

- Can rank genes by SNR

```{python}

mu_0, mu_1 = model_NB.theta_[0], model_NB.theta_[1]
var_0, var_1 = model_NB.var_[0], model_NB.var_[1]
snr = np.abs(mu_1 - mu_0) / np.sqrt(var_1 + var_0)

gene_snr_df = (
  pd.DataFrame({
    'Gene_Accession': train['Gene Accession Number'],
    'Gene_Description': train['Gene Description'],
    'SNR': snr,
    'mu_0': mu_0,
    'mu_1': mu_1,
    'sigma_0': np.sqrt(var_0),
    'sigma_1': np.sqrt(var_1)
  })
  .sort_values(by='SNR', ascending=False)
  .head(10)
  .reset_index(drop=True)
)


df_plot = gene_snr_df.reset_index(drop=True)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))

y_positions = np.arange(len(df_plot))




ax.errorbar(df_plot['mu_0'], y_positions, xerr=df_plot['sigma_0'], 
            fmt='o',  label='ALL', markersize=12,elinewidth=4)


ax.errorbar(df_plot['mu_1'], y_positions, xerr=df_plot['sigma_1'], 
            fmt='o',  label='AML', 
            elinewidth=4, markersize=12)

ylabels = [f"{gene} (SNR: {SNR:.2f})" for gene, SNR in zip(df_plot['Gene_Accession'], df_plot['SNR'])]

ax.set_yticks(y_positions)
ax.set_yticklabels(ylabels)
ax.invert_yaxis() 


ax.set_xlabel('Expression Level ($\mu \pm \sigma$)', fontsize=12)
ax.set_title('Class Expression of High SNR Genes', fontsize=24, )
ax.legend(loc='upper right', title="Cancer Type")


plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()



```
